{{short description|Circle constructed from a triangle}}
[[Image:Brocard Circle.svg|250px|right]]

In [[geometry]], the '''Brocard circle''' (or '''seven-point circle''') is a [[circle]] derived from a given triangle. It passes through the [[circumcenter]] and [[symmedian point]] of the triangle, and is centered at the midpoint of the line segment joining them (so that this segment is a [[diameter]]).

==Equation==
In terms of the side lengths <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, and <math>c</math> of the given triangle, and the [[areal coordinates]] <math>(x,y,z)</math> for points inside the triangle (where the <math>x</math>-coordinate of a point is the area of the triangle made by that point with the side of length <math>a</math>, etc), the Brocard circle consists of the points satisfying the equation<ref>{{citation
 | last = Moses
 | first = Peter J. C.
 | journal = Forum Geometricorum
 | mr = 2195737
 | pages = 97–106
 | title = Circles and triangle centers associated with the Lucas circles
 | url = https://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2005volume5/FG200513.pdf
 | volume = 5
 | year = 2005
 | access-date = 2019-01-05
 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180422182635/http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2005volume5/FG200513.pdf
 | archive-date = 2018-04-22
 | url-status = dead
 }}</ref>
:<math>b^2 c^2 x^2 + a^2 c^2 y^2 + a^2 b^2 z^2 - a^4 y z - b^4 x z - c^4 x y=0.</math>

==Related points==
The two [[Brocard points]] lie on this circle, as do the vertices of the [[Brocard triangle]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Cajori | first = Florian | author-link = Florian Cajori
 | page = 261
 | publisher = The Macmillan company
 | title = A history of elementary mathematics: with hints on methods of teaching
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=vgYCAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA261
 | year = 1917}}.</ref>
These five points, together with the other two points on the circle (the circumcenter and symmedian), justify the name "seven-point circle".

The Brocard circle is concentric with the [[Émile Lemoine#Lemoine point and circle|first Lemoine circle]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Honsberger | first = Ross | author-link = Ross Honsberger
 | isbn = 9780883856390
 | page = 110
 | publisher = Cambridge University Press
 | series = New Mathematical Library
 | title = Episodes in Nineteenth and Twentieth Century Euclidean Geometry
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=6oduPgvOAhwC&pg=PA110
 | volume = 37
 | year = 1995}}.</ref>

==Special cases==
If the triangle is [[Equilateral triangle|equilateral]], the circumcenter and symmedian coincide and therefore the Brocard circle reduces to a single point.<ref>{{citation|first=James R.|last=Smart|title=Modern Geometries|edition=5th|year=1997|publisher=Brooks/Cole|isbn=0-534-35188-3|page=184}}</ref>

==History==
The Brocard circle is named for [[Henri Brocard]],<ref>{{citation
 | last = Guggenbuhl | first = Laura
 | authorlink=Laura Guggenbuhl
 | issue = 322
 | journal = [[The Mathematical Gazette]]
 | jstor = 3610034
 | pages = 241–243
 | title = Henri Brocard and the geometry of the triangle
 | volume = 37
 | year = 1953| doi = 10.2307/3610034
 }}.</ref> who presented a paper on it to the French Association for the Advancement of Science in [[Algiers]] in 1881.<ref>{{MacTutor|title=Henri Brocard|id=Brocard}}</ref>
